equation_request.abstract: A coinless, discrete-time quantum walk possesses a Hilbert space whose dimension is smaller compared to the widely-studied coined walk. Coined walks require the direct product of the site basis with the coin space, coinless walks operate purely in the site basis, which is clearly minimal. These coinless quantum walks have received considerable attention recently because they have evolution operators that can be obtained by a graphical method based on lattice tessellations and they have been shown to be as efficient as the best known coined walks when used as a quantum search algorithm. We argue that both formulations in their most general form are equivalent. In particular, we demonstrate how to transform the one-dimensional version of the coinless quantum walk into an equivalent extended coined version for a specific family of evolution operators. We present some of its basic, asymptotic features for the one-dimensional lattice with some examples of tessellations, and analyze the mixing time and limiting probability distributions on cycles.

specification.problem: Show that coinless discrete-time quantum walks, whose evolution operators come from lattice tessellations and act only on the site basis, are equivalent to coined walks. In 1D, map the coinless walk to an extended coined walk for a specific family of evolution operators, then study its asymptotics and its mixing time and limiting distributions on cycles.
specification.reconstruction_scope: Conceptual and small finite-instance reconstruction of the 1D tessellation-based coinless walk. The abstract gives no explicit formulas, so all equations are standard background or assumed. The coined equivalence, the specific operator family and the cycle mixing results are not reconstructed.

symbols.meaning: Position (site) Hilbert space of the coinless walk
symbols.domain: span{|x>}, x in Z or Z_N

symbols.meaning: Reflection operators for the two tessellations (assumed standard form)

equations.label: Tessellation evolution operator
equations.description: The coinless step is a product of two tessellation reflection operators, each built from the polygons of one tessellation.
equations.justification: The abstract says the evolution operators come from a graphical method based on lattice tessellations. The product form is the standard construction, not stated in the abstract.

equations.label: Tessellation reflection
equations.description: Assumed 1D instance. Each polygon is a pair of adjacent sites and the reflection acts on the uniform superposition over its sites.
equations.justification: Finite instance chosen for a small example. The abstract mentions only 'some examples of tessellations'.
assumptions: Shift between tessellations by one site

equations.label: Walk state evolution
equations.description: Evolution of the state and the position probability distribution.

registers.name: pos
registers.size: n = ceil(log2 N) qubits for an N-site cycle (assumed)
registers.role: Site register; the coinless walk acts only on this register, with no coin qubit

specification.initial_state: Localized site state |0> on the position register (assumed), i.e. |psi_0> = |x=0>

steps.description: Prepare the position register in the localized state |psi_0>.
Apply the reflection H_0 for the first tessellation (pairs (2k,2k+1)).
Apply the reflection H_1 for the shifted tessellation (pairs (2k+1,2k+2)); one step is U = H_1 H_0.
Repeat the step t times to obtain |psi_t> = U^t |psi_0>.

specification.measurement: Measure the position register in the site basis after t steps, repeated over many runs to estimate p_t(x).
specification.classical_postprocessing: Build the empirical histogram of p_t(x). For cycles, compare it to the uniform distribution (for example by total variation distance) to estimate mixing behaviour, and average over t to approximate the limiting distribution.
assumptions: The 1D tessellation operator is the product of two polygon reflections, as in eq_1 and eq_2.
Polygon size 2 in 1D, with reflections as in eq_2.
The cycle has even N, and a power-of-two N is assumed for the register layout; the circuit-level implementation of H_a is not specified.
Localized initial state and an N-site cycle with a position-only register are assumed.
All equations are background or assumed; none is quoted from the abstract.
